routes.description: Establish traditional responsibility for the canonical Gospels by combining early attribution traditions with internal features linking each work to its named author or apostolic source.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the combined external and internal evidence makes Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, including authorship under their authority, the most reasonable identities behind the canonical works.

motionBridge.description: Connect the four canonical texts to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John either as writers or as controlling apostolic authorities behind their production.

centralBridges.description: Show that the early attribution tradition is sufficiently early, geographically broad, and continuous to preserve genuine authorial knowledge.
Show that internal narrative, eyewitness, linguistic, and biographical features fit the traditionally identified authors or their sources.
Show that literary dependence, Greek composition, and possible assistance are compatible with responsibility by the traditional figures.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why the comparatively less prominent names Mark and Luke are unlikely selections for a purely prestige-driven fabrication.
Apply standards for anonymous ancient works and delayed attribution consistently when assessing the Gospel traditions.

routes.description: Establish anonymous later authorship by showing that secure traditional attributions arise late, that alternative diffusion explains their unanimity, and that the named figures do not fit the texts' production.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence does not adequately identify the traditional figures as writers or controlling authorities and a later naming process better explains the surviving attributions.

motionBridge.description: Show that the canonical texts cannot be historically connected with sufficient specificity to authorship by or under the authority of the four traditional figures.

centralBridges.description: Establish a material chronological gap between Gospel composition and unambiguous attribution of the surviving canonical texts.
Establish that the traditional apostolic figures lacked the education and literary capacity required to compose the sophisticated Greek narratives.
Explain the stable fourfold naming tradition through a later authority-conferring origin and subsequent dissemination rather than independent authorial memory.
Distinguish an underlying witness or source from the final literary author and require evidence identifying the latter with a traditional figure.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether Papias, Justin, and later witnesses identify the canonical works reliably and independently.
Determine whether ancient secretarial practices support delegation of long-form Greek narrative composition in another person's name.

sectionSelections.title: Timing and continuity of external attribution
sectionSelections.rationale: The timing, independence, and geographical spread of the naming tradition determine whether it transmits authorial knowledge or reflects a convention established after the texts circulated.

proSelections.proposition: Early and geographically diverse Christian testimony consistently attributes the canonical Gospels to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, with some testimony linked to companions of apostles.

Anonymous composition and delayed explicit attribution do not defeat traditional authorship because comparable ancient works rely on similarly late testimony, while Papias and Justin provide earlier support for Mark.

conSelections.proposition: The canonical Gospels circulated without self-identification, and the first unambiguous attribution of the surviving four texts to their traditional authors appears roughly a century later.
Universal use of the four names after the late second century can derive from a common Roman naming origin and therefore does not establish that the names accompanied the Gospels from composition.

sectionSelections.title: Explanation for the traditional names
sectionSelections.rationale: Competing explanations for why these four names became stable bear directly on whether unanimity reflects inherited knowledge or an authority-conferring attribution process.

proSelections.proposition: Christians inventing prestigious Gospel attributions would not plausibly have selected the comparatively less marketable Mark and Luke instead of direct disciples.

conSelections.proposition: The traditional names were plausibly assigned late to give four previously anonymous church Gospels apostolic authority against rival writings bearing authoritative names.
Mark and Luke were useful attribution choices because they were understood as companions of Peter and Paul, completing a representation of principal apostolic witness.

sectionSelections.title: Literacy, Greek composition, and delegated production
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion requires determining whether the traditional figures could be responsible for the canonical Greek narratives, including whether assistance can bridge the asserted educational and literary mismatch.

proSelections.proposition: Verbatim Synoptic agreement fits traditional authorship because Matthew and Luke could use Mark and other reliable written sources while Matthew composed in Greek with assistance and added substantial material.

conSelections.proposition: Galilean disciples lacking elite Greek literary education could not plausibly have composed the sophisticated Greek narratives preserved as the canonical Gospels.
Ancient secretarial examples do not establish that an amanuensis composed a long, sophisticated narrative in another person's name, so they do not solve the disciples' literacy problem.

sectionSelections.title: Internal identification of Mark and Luke
sectionSelections.rationale: The proposed links between Mark and Peter and between Luke-Acts and a companion of Paul are central text-specific steps in extending traditional responsibility beyond the apostolic names.

proSelections.proposition: Mark's prominence of Peter, portrayal of Peter's personality, and preservation of Aramaic sayings fit the claim that Mark recorded material derived from Peter.
The first-person plural travel narratives in Acts indicate participation by a companion of Paul, and external testimony makes Luke the most reasonable identification of that companion-author.

conSelections.proposition: Justin's language and textual agreements are better explained by his use of the Gospel of Peter than by an attribution of canonical Mark to Peter.

sectionSelections.title: Internal identification of Matthew and John
sectionSelections.rationale: Matthew and John supply the principal apostolic identifications at issue, requiring assessment of whether internal features identify those disciples or only sources and conventionally named literary authors.

proSelections.proposition: The Fourth Gospel presents an eyewitness source identified as the beloved disciple, whose access and place among the named disciples make John son of Zebedee the best candidate.
Matthew's fiscal and Jewish features, together with early tradition, support Matthew's substantial involvement in a Greek Gospel produced from earlier Semitic material and Mark.

conSelections.proposition: Later authorship witnesses are not independent once a naming tradition begins, and John's closing distinction between the beloved disciple and a collective authorial voice weighs against direct Johannine authorship.
Matthew's references to taxes and money do not identify its author as a tax collector, because thematic vocabulary is not reliable evidence of an author's occupation.
